reason: The sources provide over a dozen mutually corroborated facts detailing the discovery, location, mechanism, and geometry of Swift J1644+57.
story: On March 28, 2011, NASA's Swift observatory detected a blinding flash in the constellation Draco, cataloged as GRB 110328A. Astronomers initially suspected an ordinary gamma-ray burst, but the blast did not fade away. Instead, it flared repeatedly with intense X-rays over several days. Observations from Swift, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and Hubble pinpointed the flare directly to the core of a distant galaxy 3.8 billion light-years away. It was not an exploding star. A dormant supermassive black hole had gravitationally ripped an approaching star to shreds. Swirling stellar debris formed an accretion disk, funneling intense magnetic fields into a relativistic particle jet traveling near light speed. By pure cosmic coincidence, this relativistic death ray was aimed directly down the barrel at Earth, boosting its observed brightness by hundreds of times and giving humanity a front-row view of a cosmic shredder.
angle: A dormant supermassive black hole 3.8 billion light-years away ripped a star to shreds and fired a relativistic jet of X-rays directly down the barrel at Earth.

claims.claim: The event was initially cataloged as gamma-ray burst GRB 110328A and later designated Swift J1644+57.
The burst was discovered on March 28, 2011.
The event was first detected by NASA's Swift satellite.
The source is located in the northern constellation Draco.
The source galaxy is situated approximately 3.8 billion light-years from Earth.
The event occurred in the center or core of a distant galaxy.
The phenomenon was a tidal disruption event caused by a supermassive black hole tearing apart a star.
Material from the shredded star fell toward the black hole in an accretion disk.
The accretion process launched a powerful particle jet traveling at relativistic speeds near the speed of light.
One of the relativistic jets pointed directly toward Earth.
The direct alignment toward Earth significantly amplified the observed brightness of the radiation.
The event generated extraordinarily luminous and long-lived X-ray emissions.
The source repeatedly flared with X-ray blasts over several days, differing from standard gamma-ray bursts.
The Chandra X-ray Observatory reoriented its schedule as a target of opportunity to observe the event in early April 2011.

disputed: Nature of the destroyed progenitor star: S1 notes timing models suggest it was possibly a white dwarf, while mass calculations match a solar-mass star; scripts should simply attribute it as a star without specifying stellar type.

Initial classification: S2 and S3 treat GRB 110328A as an anomalous GRB or evidence against standard collapse/merger models; scripts should frame the GRB designation as an initial classification that was revised to a tidal disruption event.
